hints: Start with test 1 with cold HCl. Think about which nitrogen containing groups act as bases to form soluble salts and which one is too weakly basic to dissolve.
Use test 2 with 2,4-DNPH to decide which isomers contain a C=O of an aldehyde or ketone, and use test 4 with Fehling's to split aldehyde from ketone.
Use test 3 with NaOH and I2 to pick out the very specific CH3CO group that gives the pale yellow precipitate of CHI3.
Look at test 5 with hot NaOH producing two smaller fragments. Recall which functional group breaks into an amine plus a carboxylate salt on heating with alkali.
Use test 6, diazotisation followed by coupling to give an orange dye, to decide which isomer has NH2 directly attached to the benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Sort bases from non-bases with HCl**
Think about what soluble in cold dilute acid means. Amines accept a proton to form a soluble ammonium salt, $\text{RNH}_2 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{RNH}_3^+$. J, K and L dissolve, so they contain an amine group. M is insoluble, so its nitrogen is not basic. That already points to an amide for M, where the lone pair on N is delocalised into the carbonyl and is hardly basic.

Find the carbonyls with 2,4-DNPH and Fehling's**
An orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH means an aldehyde or ketone C=O is present. J, K and L give this, M does not, which fits M as an amide rather than an aldehyde or ketone. Then warm Fehling's solution stays blue except with aldehydes, which give a red $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ precipitate. Only K gives red, so K contains an aldehyde and J and L must contain ketones.

Pin down the methyl ketone with iodoform**
The pale yellow precipitate with $\text{NaOH(aq)} + \text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$ is $\text{CHI}_3$ from the iodoform reaction, specific for $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ attached to R. J and L give it, K does not. So J and L are methyl ketones, $\text{RCOCH}_3$. K gives no reaction, consistent with an aldehyde that is not ethanal.

Confirm the amide with hot NaOH**
Only M reacts on heating with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to give two products P and Q. That is classic alkaline hydrolysis of an amide: $\text{RCONHR'} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{R'NH}_2$. So M is confirmed as an amide.

Distinguish aliphatic amine from aromatic amine**
Diazotisation with $\text{NaNO}_2$ and HCl below $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ followed by alkaline phenol gives an orange azo dye only with a primary aromatic amine, $\text{ArNH}_2$. Only K gives the dye. So K contains $\text{ArNH}_2$ directly on the ring. J and L contain amine nitrogen not directly conjugated to the ring, so they form unstable diazonium ions that do not couple to a dye.

Final answer: J: amine and methyl ketone
K: aromatic (primary aryl) amine and aldehyde
L: amine and methyl ketone
M: amide

hints: In test 5 an amide plus hot aqueous NaOH splits into two smaller molecules by adding water across the C-N bond, with NaOH consumed.
walkthrough:
Name the bond breaking process**
Picture the amide link $\text{-CONH-}$. Heating with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ breaks the C-N bond by addition of water, giving a carboxylate and an amine. That is hydrolysis, carried out under alkaline conditions.

hints: Add the atoms of P ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{N}$) and the acid part of Q together and check they rebuild the $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}$ skeleton of M plus NaOH.
Think about which fragment keeps the benzene ring as an amine and which fragment becomes the $\text{C}_3$ carboxylate salt, remembering M is an amide of a benzene amine.
walkthrough:
Assign the nitrogen fragment**
P has formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_7\text{N}$ and must contain the benzene ring plus N. That fits exactly $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, phenylamine. It is the amine released when the amide C-N bond breaks.

Assign the carboxylate fragment**
Q has formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{O}_2\text{Na}$, a sodium carboxylate with three carbons. That is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$, sodium propanoate. Together: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$, which balances and accounts for all nine carbons of M.

Final answer: P is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, phenylamine (aniline)
Q is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$, sodium propanoate

hints: Count atoms carefully. Each structure must total $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}$ with one benzene ring, leaving $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{NO}$ for the side chains.

Place the functional groups found in (a) so that J and L both contain $\text{COCH}_3$ plus an amine nitrogen in different positions, while K contains $\text{NH}_2$ on the ring plus an aldehyde side chain.
Remember M must be the amide that hydrolyses to phenylamine and propanoate, so join $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}$ directly to $\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
Look for a carbon attached to four different groups to create chirality. Only two of the four isomers are stated to be chiral.
Check that the chiral centre in K is on the side chain bearing the aldehyde and methyl groups, and in L is on the carbon bearing the amine next to the ketone.
walkthrough:
Build M first because it is fixed**
M must hydrolyse to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$. Rejoin them by removing $\text{NaOH}$ and adding back the amide link. You get $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, N-phenylpropanamide. It has no chiral carbon because $\text{CH}_2$ has two H atoms.

Build K as the aromatic amine aldehyde**
K needs $\text{H}_2\text{N}$ directly on the ring and a $-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$ side chain to total $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}$. The side chain carbon is bonded to H, $\text{CH}_3$, CHO and the aryl ring, four different groups, so it is chiral. Mark it with *. This explains the aldehyde tests and the azo dye test.

Build L as the chiral methyl ketone amine**
L needs $\text{COCH}_3$ and $\text{NH}_2$ on adjacent carbons attached to phenyl to be chiral: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-CH(NH}_2\text{)-COCH}_3$. The $\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)}$ carbon carries $\text{H}$, $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{COCH}_3$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$, so it is chiral. This gives a methyl ketone test and basic amine behaviour but no dye.

Build J as the achiral methyl ketone amine**
J has the same groups as L but must be achiral. Separate the amine and ketone so no carbon has four different groups, for example $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_2\text{COCH}_3$. Here $\text{CH}_2$ has two H atoms, so no chirality. Any isomer with formula $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}$ containing isolated $\text{COCH}_3$ and amine and no chiral centre is acceptable.

Check the two chiral isomers rule**
Only K and L have a carbon with four different substituents. J and M have $\text{CH}_2$ groups or planar amide N, so they are achiral. Always draw the * clearly on the $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$ carbon of K and the $\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)}$ carbon of L.

Final answer: J is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_2\text{COCH}_3$ (or isomeric $\text{CH}_3\text{NHC}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCH}_3$ or $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCH}_3$)
K is $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$ with * on $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$ carbon
L is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-CH(NH}_2\text{)-COCH}_3$ with * on $\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)}$ carbon
M is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$
K and L only show chiral centres as marked

hints: Think about what happens when the aldehyde side chain in K is oxidised under alkaline conditions and cleaved to leave the benzoate ion.
walkthrough:
Identify the oxidation fragment**
Strong oxidation of the aldehyde containing side chain removes the side chain carbons and leaves the benzene ring as a carboxylate salt under alkaline conditions. The $\text{C}_7$ product $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ is sodium benzoate, with $\text{CO}_2^-$ directly on the ring.
Final answer: W is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$, sodium benzoate
